title: 'SharedRoot' escape lets Claude Cowork read the host Mac's SSH keys and cloud credentials
subtitle: Accomplish researcher Oren Yomtov chained a kernel bug and a writable VirtioFS mount to break out of Anthropic's local agent sandbox in one message; Anthropic classified the report 'informative.'
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Security researcher Oren Yomtov at Accomplish AI publicly disclosed a full sandbox-escape vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Cowork, dubbed 'SharedRoot.' Yomtov demonstrated that connecting a folder to a fresh Cowork session and sending one short message caused the agent to break out of its Linux VM and read and write files across the host macOS — including SSH private keys, cloud credentials and any file the logged-in user could access. The attack chain combined CVE-2026-46331, a Linux kernel bug in the act_pedit traffic-control subsystem (nicknamed 'pedit COW'), with a writable VirtioFS mount at /mnt/.virtiofs-root that exposed the entire host filesystem to guest root.

The affected population is not small. Approximately 500,000 macOS users ran local Cowork sessions before Anthropic moved the product to default cloud execution, which sidesteps this specific escape path. Anthropic closed Yomtov's submission as 'Informative' — the lowest severity rating in its disclosure program — and did not ship a targeted patch, arguing that the cloud transition mitigates the issue in practice. Yomtov disputes that framing: the local VM was the product's default advertised deployment for months, and the exposure window was real. The disagreement is a preview of what agent-sandbox disclosure fights are going to look like as more labs ship desktop agents.

The broader lesson is about the sandbox model itself. VirtioFS-style writable host mounts are a common shortcut when a vendor wants an agent to feel fast and useful — the agent can save files back to your Downloads folder, for example. That same shortcut is what SharedRoot exploited. Any agent product that promises full local computer control needs to solve the tradeoff explicitly: strict isolation with clunky file-passing, or convenient mounts with the residual risk of exactly this class of bug. OpenAI's ChatGPT Voice desktop launch on July 23 uses a similar architecture, and independent researchers are already probing it. Expect more disclosures of this shape in Q3.

For learners: if you use any AI agent that can 'access your files' locally, ask what it is running inside. A container, a VM, a browser extension and a native process all have very different security postures — and vendor marketing will not tell you which one you are getting. The right question is: what happens if the model does exactly what the attacker asks? If the answer involves your SSH keys, use the cloud-hosted version, or don't connect anything sensitive to it. That is not a permanent rule — the sandbox tech will get better — but it is the right rule until at least Q4.
